Executive summary

Small cafes need a consistent way to receive pickup orders without relying on verbal messages or handwritten lists. DashFood provides a responsive web menu, a persistent cart and a checkout connected to a shared PostgreSQL database. Customers submit a pickup name, receive an order reference and follow preparation status. Authenticated staff process the same order, change menu availability and inspect aggregated order data. The final build retains the original project scope and corrects issues identified in the earlier review: hidden mobile navigation, searches containing extra spaces and an edit form that opened outside the viewport. It also protects customer order lookup with a secret tracking key and prevents duplicate orders when a checkout request is retried. Verification covers database operations, customer and staff journeys, mobile layout, accessibility scanning and controlled page-load measurements. The data analysis uses labelled seeded records and synthetic verification orders, so its charts demonstrate a repeatable method rather than real cafe demand. External participants tested the earlier build according to the team, but their task completion times were not recorded. The final assessment therefore separates demonstrated software behaviour from pending human timing, deployment trust and long-term availability evidence.

Review edition. The system and automated evidence are complete for this build. Human timing, individual signatures and deployment/availability evidence remain explicit open items. No separate team name was supplied; DashFood is the project name.

Problem, scope and evidence

Stage 1 identifies a practical ordering problem: customers need to see products and prices before arriving, while staff need one reliable list of pickup orders. A verbal order can lose an item or require repetition. DashFood records the selected products and gives both user groups a shared status.

What the evidence supports

EvidenceSupported conclusionLimit

Stage 2, final five pagesThree reproducible interface problems and instrumented page-load resultsNot a timed human checkout study

Team clarificationMedet, Nurdaulet and Iskander participated in testingTask times and individual observations were not supplied

Scope retained

The finished scope covers menu browsing, prices, cart changes, pickup checkout, status tracking, staff order processing and menu control. Insights and a simulated queue rule reuse the same data. Customers pay at pickup. Payroll, delivery tracking, supplier management, reservations, loyalty and online card payments remain outside the project.

Operational outcome

The demonstrated result is an auditable handoff from customer selection to staff preparation. Queue reduction and sales improvement remain hypotheses until a real cafe measures comparable before/after conditions. The final report does not convert a functioning prototype into an unsupported business-impact claim.

Three original success criteria

SC1: a customer places an order in less than two minutes. SC2: an unavailable product cannot enter a new order. SC3: the main ordering interface works at a width of 360 pixels. These come from Stage 1 page 5. The three important requirements on page 8 (R1, R3, R6) are a different list.

Page-load time measures the interface becoming ready. Human task time includes reading, choosing, typing and understanding the confirmation. These metrics cannot substitute for one another. No human time under 120 seconds is claimed.

Cost and performance justification

The review uses existing hardware and open-source software. No paid cloud account is required for the local demonstration. Electricity, hardware, internet and future hosting still have costs; no zero-cost production claim is made. The revised final report removes the outdated AWS 12-month free-tier assertion.

A single application process and connection pool keep the demonstration simple. PostgreSQL indexes support order-item joins and chronological queries. Responsive WebP variants reduce image bytes. Current browser measurements assess the actual production build; they do not establish capacity for 10,000 concurrent users.

Data model and transaction design

TableImportant columnsPurpose / relationship
usersid, username, password_hash, roleUnique staff account; bcrypt password hash
productsid, name, category, price, description, activeWhole positive KZT; fixed category check
ordersid, total, status, created_at, customer_name, is_demoOne pickup transaction and its current state
orders: final additionstracking_hash, request_key, request_hashCustomer read authorization and retry deduplication
order_itemsid, order_id, name, price, qtyMany items per order; FK to orders with cascading delete
seed_batchesname, created_atMarks one repeatable synthetic seed batch

Checkout transaction

The API validates the pickup name and unique product lines. It locks one checkout request key using a transaction-level advisory lock, then checks for a prior order. Repeating the same payload returns the saved receipt; changing that payload with the same key returns a conflict. The server reads active product rows with a shared lock, obtains their names/prices and calculates the total.

It inserts orders and order_items, commits them together, then returns the receipt. Failures roll back the transaction. Row locks prevent a concurrent menu edit from changing price or availability midway through this write. A unique index is an additional guard on request_key.

Historical correctness

Each order item retains the purchased name, price and quantity. Editing a menu price later does not rewrite an old receipt. Integer KZT avoids floating-point currency rounding in this scope. Quantity is limited to 50 per product and the total to 10,000,000 KZT. Parameterized queries treat customer text as data.

The schema is additive for existing installations. Legacy orders without a tracking hash remain staff-visible but cannot be opened publicly by guessing their IDs. No old customer tracking credentials are fabricated.

Security, privacy and failure handling

RiskImplemented controlRemaining limit
Staff impersonationbcrypt hashes, HS256 JWT verification, eight-hour expiry, login rate limitNo MFA or managed account administration
Guessing another orderSecret token returned at checkout; only SHA-256 token hash stored; constant-time comparisonBrowser storage must be retained and protected
Price manipulationPrices read from DB; customer-supplied total ignoredNo inventory reservation or online payment
Double checkout after lost responsePersistent checkout key and serialized server retriesDifferent keys represent different orders
Malformed input or SQL injectionJSON size cap, type/range checks, parameterized SQL, valid identifiersNo claim of a complete penetration test
Invalid staff actionsAtomic state transition guards; terminal statuses cannot jump backwardsOne admin role, no detailed staff audit log

Personal data and location

Pickup names are stored in the PostgreSQL orders table and shown only to authenticated staff. Customer order read omits the name. The application collects no phone, address or payment-card details. In this review, DB files reside on the laptop under .local; in Docker they reside in a named volume on the deployment host. No cloud location is assumed.

Before real use, the operator needs a documented hosting location, retention/deletion policy, encrypted backups and an appropriate review of Kazakhstan personal-data obligations. Local synthetic testing does not establish legal compliance. The final build does not claim automatic AES-256 encryption of database files.

Visible recovery

Errors keep the cart intact, unavailable items can be removed, and retries preserve the checkout key. A missing receipt no longer prevents other customer orders from loading. Expired staff sessions return to sign-in. Non-API routes serve the app, while unknown API routes return JSON 404.

Customer interface and multimedia

The menu exposes names, descriptions, categories and KZT prices before checkout. Search ignores surrounding spaces. Repeated add actions announce visible feedback and update cart quantity/total. Cart controls support removal and a 1-50 quantity range. Checkout asks for a pickup name and explains payment at the cafe.

Media and accessibility decisions

Images use local WebP variants, explicit dimensions, srcSet/sizes and descriptive alternative text. The hero image loads eagerly; non-priority cards can load lazily. Unknown products receive a stable fallback. Credits remain in the linked local media credits page. Example photography is not presented as actual cafe stock.

Main buttons have minimum heights of 44 or 48 CSS pixels. Keyboard focus is visible. Reduced-motion preference disables animations and smooth scrolling. Text appears on opaque surfaces rather than photographs. Brand text #1854ed on white has a calculated contrast of 5.95:1; secondary text #5d6a82 on white is 5.46:1. Ratios use the WCAG sRGB luminance formula.

Automated accessibility scanning covers six screens at 360px. It cannot certify every screen-reader experience. User-controlled backup video is a separate presentation artifact; the application plays no automatic audio.

Staff journey and customer handoff

Staff sign in to see the same PostgreSQL order created by the customer. The required workflow is New, Preparing, Ready and Completed. Cancellation is allowed from New or Preparing. Attempts to skip stages or update an already changed order are rejected. Busy controls reduce accidental repeated actions.

Manage menu supports creating a product, editing name/description/category/whole KZT price and toggling availability. An unavailable product disappears from public menu responses and cannot be purchased from a stale cart. Editing the last product scrolls to the form and focuses its Name field; Cancel restores the original Edit button.

Two user groups in one demonstration

The live presentation must show both journeys: customer checkout and tracking, then staff processing and menu control. Showing only the home page does not demonstrate the shared database. Use the created order number to connect the browser action, the staff card and the SQL query.

Smart extension and its limits

Implemented simulation

Insights calculates an estimated waiting time using min(60, 5 + 3 x active orders) minutes. Active means New or Preparing. The screen refreshes every eight seconds and explicitly states that no physical sensor is connected. Staff actions change the queue and therefore the estimate.

Active ordersCalculated estimateMeaning
05 minutesFixed baseline
314 minutes5 + 3 x 3
2060 minutesUncapped 65 reaches the 60-minute limit

The formula is a transparent software rule. It has not been calibrated against kitchen preparation times and must not be presented as an accurate promise to customers. The menu hero should avoid treating a fixed promotional estimate as a measured live value.

Future anonymous occupancy counter

A possible extension uses a time-of-flight pickup counter, Wi-Fi with per-device credentials, authenticated HTTPS ingestion and a sensor_readings table. The staff screen would combine aggregate occupancy with the current queue. No camera, face recognition or phone identifiers are needed for this proposed design.

At one reading per ten seconds, a device sends 8,640 readings per day. Assuming 100 bytes of JSON per reading gives about 0.864 MB of raw JSON, excluding network overhead, retries and storage indexes. A future retention proposal is seven days for raw data and 30 days for minute aggregates. These are design assumptions, not deployed collection or retention policies.

Failure modes

Connectivity loss needs a stale-data indicator; duplicate sequence numbers need deduplication; impossible counts need rejection. New presence patterns may still affect privacy even without names. No sensor-ingestion route, hardware test or production accuracy is claimed.

Deployment, reproducibility and recovery

One local review command

Install dependencies with npm run setup, then run npm run review. It compiles the app, starts a persistent local PostgreSQL 16 instance, applies additive schema changes, inserts the seed batch once and starts HTTP/TLS endpoints. StartPreview.cmd provides the Windows entry point. The README lists the guest and staff role credentials and where generated passwords live.

Alternative Docker path

Open Docker Desktop and run setup.ps1 on Windows or bash setup.sh on macOS/Linux. App and database health checks verify the connection. A named volume persists data across ordinary stops. The optional Caddy profile accepts an owned domain for HTTPS. Docker was not available in the assessment session, so the final verified execution uses native local PostgreSQL rather than claiming a fresh container deployment.

Backup and restore exercise

For Docker, an operator can export with docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U cafe -d cafe and save the output securely. Rehearse restoration into a separate test database before relying on a backup. A backup is sensitive because it contains pickup names. Do not publish it or store it in Git. Ordinary restart must preserve existing orders.

Availability measurement

tools/monitor.mjs records timestamped health responses, latency, expected sample count and the observed window. A meaningful R15 assessment needs a declared duration and inclusion of missed probes during downtime. Restart policies and a successful launch demonstrate recovery mechanisms; they do not by themselves establish 99% uptime.

Repository evidence

Existing history remains intact. The final work stays on a local review branch until approved. GitHub Actions is configured to run build, API and browser/accessibility checks using PostgreSQL 16. Remote execution is pending push; no green remote checks or new participant commits are invented.

Future engineering work

Before a real cafe launch, add explicit data-retention controls, backup/restore verification, stronger operator account management and monitoring. A higher-load deployment would need bounded/paginated staff order queries, rate limits on public ordering, measured load tests and a capacity plan. The current aggregate queries and unbounded staff list are likely scaling pressure points.

No inventory, delivery, card payment or calibrated kitchen forecast is supplied. These omissions retain the original pickup scope. The most useful immediate work is completing evidence and practicing the existing system rather than adding another feature before defense.

A functioning build and polished report cannot substitute for measurements, personal signatures or a live explanation. Pending criteria remain visible in the final requirement and test tables.
